title: The rule at work
hook: which parts of your rule travel to work? Abba Hilkiah keeps hoeing, and Baizhang won't eat on a day without work
tomorrow: in Genesis, what came before the very first job?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: my rule, read aloud and stood to. The building block is closed. Now the rule leaves home, and its first stop is work.

Monday morning, the laptop opening, and the long sit you planned feels like something from another life. The Talmud tells of a drought, and of a man named Abba Hilkiah whose prayers, people said, brought rain. The rabbis sent two scholars to ask him to pray. They found him hoeing in a field. They greeted him. He didn't answer, and he didn't look up.
screen: `MONDAY, THE LAPTOP OPENING.` → `A DROUGHT, AND A MAN WHO PRAYS.` → `HE DIDN'T LOOK UP.`

segments.voice: He worked to the end of the day and walked home. Only then did he and his wife go up to the roof to pray, and the clouds came. Afterward the scholars asked why he hadn't returned their greeting. His answer, in substance: I was hired by the day, and I wouldn't take my employer's time. That small story carries a real Jewish teaching: a worker's hours belong to the one who pays for them, and Jewish law makes room for prayer inside those hours. The Mishnah says craftsmen may recite the Shema right where they are, at the top of a tree or on a course of stones, without climbing down. The prayer comes to the job, in a form that fits it. So, today's question: which parts of a rule travel to work? This tradition's answer: the parts that fit inside honest work without stealing from it. Now a neighbor. The Chan master Baizhang, tradition says, kept working in the monastery fields into old age. When his monks hid his tools so he would rest, he wouldn't eat that day: a day without work, a day without food. What's shared: both hold honest work as part of a holy life. The honest difference: Baizhang's monks made the work itself the practice, while the Mishnah keeps prayer and paid work distinct, and fits the prayer around hours that belong to someone else.
screen: `HIRED BY THE DAY.` · `THE SHEMA AT THE TOP OF A TREE.` · `WHAT FITS HONEST WORK TRAVELS.` · `BAIZHANG: NO WORK, NO FOOD.` · then, large: `THE RULE FITS THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Sit the way you sit at your desk, hands where the keyboard would be. Go through your rule part by part and ask whether it fits inside your work hours without stealing from them. Pick one part that does, and rest with it as the part that travels.
The rule at work: the parts of your rule that travel to your job, fitted inside honest work. Abba Hilkiah prayed after the hoeing.
For Monday: at work, the part that fits without stealing anyone's time. Day 1707, and the rule goes out the door.

screen: `DAY 1707 COUNTS.` → `AT WORK · 1 OF 7.` → `TOMORROW: IN GENESIS, WHAT CAME BEFORE THE VERY FIRST JOB?`

howItsDone: The Mishnah allows workers to recite the Shema where they are working, and Jewish law treats an employer's hours as owed; in Chan monasteries, work in the fields was part of the monks' practice. On a personal rule, one short part is chosen to travel to work.

chat.says: back at work tomorrow. my rule has a long morning sit. which part of it even comes with me?
options: what fits honest work. workers in the Mishnah say the Shema up the tree. bring a short form.
all of it. do the full sit at your desk on company time; your practice comes first.
none of it. work is work and practice is practice; keep the rule at home completely.
chat.meaning: Abba Hilkiah wouldn't take time owed to his employer, and the Mishnah lets workers pray where they stand. What travels to work is what fits honest work.

Abba Hilkiah.meaning: a laborer in the Talmud whose prayers were said to bring rain

Mishnah.meaning: the early code of Jewish law that the Talmud discusses

Shema.meaning: the Jewish declaration that begins Hear, O Israel

Chan.meaning: the Chinese school of Buddhism known in Japan as Zen

Baizhang.meaning: a Chan master remembered for working the fields with his monks

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a-b (Abba Hilkiah hoeing in the field; does not return the scholars' greeting; prays with his wife on the roof; hired by the day, he would not interrupt his work)
Mishnah Berakhot 2:4 (craftsmen may recite the Shema at the top of a tree or on a course of stones)
Baizhang Huaihai, as told in the Chan records (Transmission of the Lamp): the hidden tools; 'a day without work, a day without food'
